newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius bourse mulls bond, treasury bill market.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius bourse mulls bond, treasury bill market.

text.p: Secondary markets in bonds and treasury bills are on the cards for Mauritius, and preliminary talks have already taken place with the central bank and government, stock exchange officials said.

Richard Morin, the Stock Exchange of Mauritius's (SEM) chief executive, said that if everything ran smoothly the Indian Ocean island could have two new markets by the end of 1998, allowing government primary issues to be traded.
"It is one of the objectives of the stock exchange to work with government to develop a truly effective market for bonds and T-bills," he said in an interview.

"We are still in very preliminary discussions. But it could be done very rapidly ... (A Mauritian bond and T-bill market) by the end of 1998 is very realistic. It is realistic to do much of the work in 1997."
The exchange had already had talks with the Mauritius central bank and the finance ministry and put forward specific proposals on how to develop the new markets, he said.

Much of the infrastructure for the efficient running of the markets was already in place. SEM in January launched a modern central depositary and settlement firm where trades are settled on a rolling T+5 basis.
But Michael Lim, the chairman of SEM, said a number of stumbling blocks needed to be cleared before the markets could take off.
These included winning the support of government, a shortage of skills in the small country of just over one million people, ignorance about debt markets and a dearth of potential market players.
"We only have a few domestic banks," he told Reuters in a separate interview.

He said the number of institutional participants could be increased if an overhaul of the country's pensions industry, which has shied away from investing in securities, was carried out simultaneously.

Government, which had only been in power for a short time might also not have had enough time to fully digest the nuances of the financial sector, he said. It also, for the moment, had its eye fixed on more pressing matters like the June 9 budget.
"The government has to first reorganise the primary market for us to be able to play our role in the secondary market," Morin said.
"The machinery is there, it's a question of how the Treasury uses that machinery to develop the market."
